name: Ioannidis counts the false positives
scope: The paper that indicted the literature from inside the establishment's own press. T1: in August 2005 the journal PLoS Medicine printed an article whose TITLE read like a charge sheet -- 'Why Most Published Research Findings Are False' -- and it went on to become the most-downloaded paper the journal had ever run and has since been cited over 10,000 times; the author was Stanford physician-epidemiologist John Ioannidis (the hook is the title, printed by medicine's own side). T2: Ioannidis ran no experiment and collected no new data -- he did arithmetic ON the literature itself, asking a question nobody was asking: of all the 'significant' findings that reach print, what fraction are actually true? T3 (the mechanism rung; teach 'positive predictive value' first): picture 1,000 hypotheses tested of which only 100 are really true; at the standard 5% false-positive rate and 80% power you harvest about 80 true hits AND about 45 false hits -- roughly a third of your 'discoveries' are noise before anyone cheats at all. T4: corollary one -- the SMALLER the study, the less likely its finding is true, because small samples swing wildly and only the lucky swings clear p<0.05. T5: corollary four -- the more FLEXIBILITY a field allows in design, definitions and analysis, the less likely its findings are true. T6: corollary five -- the greater the financial interest and prejudice in a field, the less likely its findings are true. T7: the corollary nobody expects -- the HOTTER the field, the worse it gets: when many teams race the same question, the first to hit significance publishes, so the racing itself manufactures false positives. T8: Ioannidis later put a number on the filter -- surveys of the biomedical literature found over 96% of reported p-values were 'significant', which is not what honest testing looks like; it is what a shelf looks like after the nulls have been strained out. T9 (the self-scrutiny rung the bank must include): the paper has been CHALLENGED, not refuted -- Jager and Leek's 2014 reanalysis of reported p-values in top medical journals estimated a false-discovery rate nearer 14%, and Goodman and Greenland argued the model rested on plausible-but-chosen assumptions rather than measured ones; Ioannidis answered in print and the argument is live. T10: what the paper never said -- it did not say science is worthless; it said the FILTER is weak, and it named the repairs (bigger studies, pre-specified analyses, honesty about how long a shot the hypothesis was). T11: the durable lesson -- 'it was published in a peer-reviewed journal' is a fact about a manuscript's reception, not about how the world works; the only thing that settles it is somebody running it again.
source: Grokipedia 'Replication crisis' (grokipedia.com/page/Replication_crisis); Grokipedia 'John Ioannidis' (grokipedia.com/page/John_Ioannidis) -- confirms PLOS Medicine 2005, >10,000 citations, the PPV model, the corollaries, the >96%-significant p-value surveys, METRICS/Stanford; Wikipedia 'Why Most Published Research Findings Are False' -- the six corollaries verbatim, and the Goodman/Greenland/Jager/Leek critique with the ~14% counter-estimate; primary: Ioannidis JPA, PLoS Med 2(8):e124 (2005).
framing_note: KEYSTONE of the whole sub-strand -- every other replication ladder leans on it. VOICE: no sneering at scientists; Ioannidis's own claim is that honest, competent researchers generate false positives BECAUSE of the incentive structure, not because they lie. PRESENT, never preach. ACCURACY RAIL (the one that matters): no rung may claim the paper 'proved most science is false' or was 'never refuted' -- it is a MODEL, its exact percentage is contested, and T9 exists to say so out loud. That rung IS the bank's voice: Feynman's 'you must not fool yourself' applied to the bank's own favorite paper. Name the journal and title exactly (PLoS Medicine, 2005) -- never 'a medical journal'. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF: T3 -- a kid can work the 1,000-hypotheses count on paper and watch a third of the 'discoveries' turn to noise with nobody cheating. DISTRACTOR MINE: real adjacent metascientists and their real contributions -- Brian Nosek (the Reproducibility Project), Robert Rosenthal (the file drawer), Jacob Cohen (statistical power), Ronald Fisher (p<0.05 itself), Doug Altman ('the scandal of poor medical research') -- plus real rival journals (Nature, Science, JAMA, The Lancet, NEJM). Never joke options. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let a stem say 'small studies are unreliable' and then ask what the corollary was -- describe the SCENE (a paper with no new data, only arithmetic) and let the corollary be recalled knowledge.
history_overlap: SCIENCE-INTERNAL: the COVID sub-strand owns Ioannidis's March 2020 'a fiasco in the making?' essay and the Santa Clara seroprevalence fight -- this ladder keys the 2005 PAPER and its mathematics only, and must not re-tell the COVID episode. PHILOSOPHY bank owns Bayes/base rates as an abstract reasoning move -- keep T3 anchored to Ioannidis's own 1,000-hypotheses accounting, not a generic Bayes lesson.

name: Only 36 of 100
scope: The audit that broke psychology open. T1: starting in 2011, some 270 researchers spent four years re-running 100 published psychology experiments drawn from three top journals; 97 of the originals had reported a statistically significant result -- only 36 of the re-runs did (the hook is the pair of numbers: 97 in, 36 out). T2: the act itself was the novelty -- nobody had ever systematically checked; the effort was organized by Brian Nosek through the Open Science Collaboration and the Center for Open Science, which he had founded in 2013, and it appeared in Science in 2015. T3: the second number, worse than the first -- even where an effect survived, it SHRANK by about half (mean correlation 0.403 in the originals, 0.197 in the replications). The literature was not merely wrong sometimes; it was systematically inflated. T4: the fields were not equal -- cognitive psychology (memory, attention) replicated at roughly 50%, social psychology at roughly 25%. The closer a finding sat to a stopwatch and the further from a story about human nature, the better it held. T5 (the defense, and why it collapsed): the standard reply was 'hidden moderators' -- the effect is real but delicate, and needs our students, our lab, our country. Many Labs 2 (2018) tested that directly: 28 classic effects run across 28 laboratories on over 15,000 people. When an effect replicated it replicated nearly EVERYWHERE, and when it failed it failed nearly everywhere. Fragility was not the explanation. T6: the corroboration nobody could dismiss as a psychology problem -- a 2016 Nature survey of 1,576 working scientists found more than 70% had tried and failed to reproduce another scientist's experiment, and more than half had failed to reproduce their OWN (87% of chemists, 77% of biologists, 69% of physicists and engineers). T7: the mechanism underneath, not fraud but arithmetic -- these were small studies chasing small effects, and a small study only clears the significance bar when chance has already pushed the number too far. T8: what a failed replication does NOT mean -- it is not proof the original was faked, and it is not proof the effect is absent; it means the evidence we had was not evidence. Saying that plainly is the discipline. T9: the response that proves the tradition works -- psychology did not bury the result; it published it in Science, in its own flagship, and then rebuilt its methods in public. T10: the standing lesson for a reader of headlines -- 'a study found' is the beginning of a claim's life, not the end of it; the question that separates knowledge from news is 'has anyone run it again?'
source: Grokipedia 'Replication crisis' -- 100 studies from three 2008 journals, 97% originally significant vs 36% replicating, r 0.403 -> 0.197, social 23% vs cognitive ~48%, Many Labs 2 (28 labs / 36 samples / 28 effects, ~50%), Center for Open Science and OSF preregistration from 2013; Wikipedia 'Reproducibility Project' -- the three journals named (Psychological Science, JPSP, JEP:LMC), Nosek, launch November 2011; Wikipedia 'Replication crisis' -- Baker's 2016 Nature survey of 1,576 researchers with the per-discipline breakdown, and the Many Labs 2 'consistent across contexts' finding; primary: Open Science Collaboration, Science 349:aac4716 (2015).
framing_note: The flagship DISCOVERY-as-audit ladder: the named act (270 people re-running 100 studies) carries T1, not a definition of replication. VOICE: admiration, not schadenfreude -- the people who ran this audit are the heroes of the ladder, and the field that published its own bad news is behaving like science. ACCURACY RAIL: 36% is the rate of replications reaching statistical significance in the same direction; it is NOT '64% of psychology is fake' and no rung may say so. State the 97/36 pair together so the comparison is honest, and keep T8 (what a failed replication does not mean) as a mandatory rung -- without it the ladder teaches nihilism, which is the failure mode this bank must not have. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF: T1 (97 in, 36 out) and T5 (when it works it works everywhere; when it fails it fails everywhere). DISTRACTOR MINE: real adjacent explanations that serious people offered and that are wrong here -- hidden moderators, cultural differences, experimenter skill, 'the effect is real but fragile', decline effect -- plus real named projects a player could confuse (Many Labs, the Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology, ManyBabies, the Psychological Science Accelerator) and real journals. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: describe the SCENE (four years, 270 researchers, 100 studies pulled from 2008 issues) and let the number be recalled -- never put '36%' in a stem that then asks what the project found.
history_overlap: PHILOSOPHY bank owns falsifiability and Popper as epistemology -- this ladder keys the physical ACT of re-running 100 named studies and what the tally showed, never the seminar argument. No sister-bank fact duplicated.

name: The effects that dissolved on re-test
scope: THEME ladder across the three most famous collapses -- one wonder per rung, the theme being 'a small first study, a beautiful story, a huge audience, and then somebody ran it again'. T1: Amy Cuddy's 2012 TED talk telling people to stand like Wonder Woman for two minutes before a job interview became one of the two most-watched TED talks ever (roughly 47 million views by 2017) -- and it rested on a single 2010 Psychological Science study of 42 undergraduates. T2: what that study claimed was not a feeling but CHEMISTRY -- two minutes of 'high power' posture raised testosterone, lowered cortisol, and made people gamble more. T3: the re-test (Ranehill and colleagues, Psychological Science 2015, a much larger Zurich sample) split the claim in half: the self-reported FEELING of power survived; the hormones and the risk-taking did not. T4 (the rarest act in science): in September 2016 the original study's FIRST author, Dana Carney, posted a public statement on her own faculty page -- 'I do not believe that "power pose" effects are real' -- and listed the analytic choices in her own data that had produced them. T5: ego depletion, the 1998 experiment -- participants sat in a room with warm chocolate-chip cookies and a bowl of radishes; those told to eat only the radishes later gave up sooner on an unsolvable puzzle. Willpower looked like a fuel tank you could run dry. T6: the idea governed self-help and psychology for fifteen years, and a 2010 meta-analysis of 198 tests put the effect at a solid d of about 0.6, declaring it extremely unlikely to be absent. T7: the re-test -- a 2016 Registered Replication Report in which about two dozen laboratories ran ONE protocol agreed in advance on 2,141 participants and found essentially nothing. T8: the warning that had already been printed -- Carter and McCullough's 2014 reanalysis showed that once the 2010 meta-analysis was corrected for publication bias the effect fell to about d = 0.2 and could no longer be told from zero. The alarm was in the literature before the replication ran. T9: social priming -- Bargh, Chen and Burrows (1996) had students unscramble sentences seeded with words like Florida, bingo and wrinkle, and then measured how fast they walked down the corridor afterwards. The primed students walked more slowly. T10: the re-test with better instruments -- Doyen and colleagues (PLOS ONE, 2012) timed 120 walkers with infrared beams instead of a human with a stopwatch, and found nothing. T11 (the mechanism rung, and the payoff): then they ran a second, diabolical experiment -- they TOLD ten experimenters which condition each subject was in. The slow walk appeared only for experimenters who expected slowness, and only on the human-operated stopwatches; the infrared beams saw no difference. The effect was in the experimenter's thumb. T12: in 2012 Daniel Kahneman -- who had championed priming in his own book -- sent an open letter to the priming field warning of a train wreck looming and telling them to organize replications themselves before others did it for them. T13: the honest close -- across all three collapses, nobody has shown fraud. Small samples, flexible analysis, and an audience that wanted the story were enough.
source: Wikipedia 'Power posing' -- Carney/Cuddy/Yap 2010 Psychological Science, N=42, testosterone/cortisol claim, ~47M TED views by 2017, Ranehill et al. 2015 (feelings replicated, physiology and behaviour did not), Carney's 2016 statement quoted, Simmons & Simonsohn p-curve 2016; Wikipedia 'Ego depletion' -- Baumeister et al. 1998 JPSP radish/chocolate design, Hagger et al. 2010 meta-analysis d=.6 over 198 tests, Hagger et al. 2016 RRR (~2 dozen labs, 2,141 participants, no evidence), Carter & McCullough 2014 (d falls to .2); PubMed abstract of Baumeister, Bratslavsky, Muraven & Tice 1998 (JPSP) -- 'quit faster on unsolvable puzzles'; Wikipedia 'Priming (psychology)' -- Bargh/Chen/Burrows 1996 word list and walking speed, Kahneman's open letter and his 2022 'effectively dead' remark; PLOS ONE 7(1):e29081 (Doyen, Klein, Pichon & Cleeremans 2012) abstract -- Exp 1 n=120 with infrared timing and no effect, Exp 2 n=50 with 10 experimenters primed for 'Slow'/'Fast', effect present only under expectancy and only on manual chronometry; Grokipedia 'Replication crisis' -- priming replicating in ~17% of 94 studies, ego depletion succeeding in 4 of 36 multi-site attempts.
framing_note: THEME ladder (shape B) -- the theme is 'the famous effect that dissolved', displayed across three named cases; each rung must be ONE case's ONE fact, never a stack. VOICE: absolutely no sneering and no cartoon villains. Cuddy, Baumeister and Bargh are real scientists who were not shown to have faked anything, and the ladder is stronger if it says so (T13 is mandatory). The recognition skill being taught is METHOD vs CELEBRITY, not 'psychologists are frauds'. ACCURACY RAILS (three, all load-bearing): (1) Ranehill 2015 replicated the FELT sense of power -- only the hormones and risk-taking failed; never write 'power posing does nothing'. (2) The 2016 ego-depletion RRR found no effect, but the theory is contested rather than formally 'disproven' -- some researchers still defend it; say 'the best-designed test found nothing'. (3) Doyen's own stated conclusion is that BOTH priming and experimenter expectancy were instrumental -- do not claim they proved priming is fake. VERIFY AT BUILD: Ranehill's exact N (~200), the RRR lab count (commonly given as 23), the TED view count, and the exact wording and date of Kahneman's 2012 letter and Carney's 2016 statement -- both are real documented quotes, so quote them exactly or paraphrase, never invent. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF: T11, the experimenter's thumb -- the single most transferable fact in the sub-strand, and the natural doorway to why blinding exists. DISTRACTOR MINE: real psychology that DID hold up -- the Stroop effect, semantic priming, the spacing effect, cognitive-load effects -- plus the real rival explanations offered at the time (hidden moderators, cultural difference, experimenter skill, 'real but fragile'). Adjacent-and-true is what makes these hard. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let a stem name the instrument (infrared vs stopwatch) before asking what Doyen found; describe the corridor and the ten experimenters and let the finding be recalled.
history_overlap: PHILOSOPHY bank may own appeal-to-authority and celebrity-as-evidence as fallacy moves -- keep every rung here anchored to the named study and its numbers, never to a fallacy label. SCIENCE-INTERNAL: the blinding/controls ladder elsewhere in this bank owns Mesmer and Clever Hans -- T11 must key DOYEN'S experiment specifically and may gesture at blinding only as the repair, not re-tell Clever Hans.

name: Bem's precognition paper lights the fuse
scope: The reductio that started the crisis. T1: in 2011 the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology -- psychology's flagship -- published nine experiments by Cornell's Daryl Bem reporting that ordinary students could feel the future: they picked the curtain hiding an erotic image slightly more often than chance BEFORE the computer had chosen where to put it. T2: Bem was not a crank on the fringe; he was a respected social psychologist and a methods teacher, and he got in by using the field's own standard equipment -- ordinary sample sizes, ordinary analyses, p<0.05 -- which is precisely why it detonated. T3 (the logical move that made it historic): if the discipline's accepted method can produce publishable evidence for something physically impossible, then the fault is not in the finding -- it is in the METHOD. Bem had, accidentally, run the best possible test of psychology's toolkit. T4: what happened next was worse than the paper -- Stuart Ritchie, Richard Wiseman and Chris French re-ran one of the experiments, found nothing, and were rejected by JPSP, by Science Brevia and by Psychological Science on the stated grounds that it was a replication. T5: the British Journal of Psychology sent it out to a referee, and the referee was Bem himself, who flagged the conflict of interest; it was rejected there too. The file-drawer machine had been caught operating in daylight. T6: the statistical autopsy -- Wagenmakers and colleagues showed Bem had reported one-sided p-values where two-sided were required and that a Bayesian reading of his own data favoured no effect; Francis and Schimmack showed that nine significant results out of ten was itself too clean to be honest sampling. T7: Bem's own words to Slate in 2017 -- 'I'm all for rigor, but I prefer other people do it... I used data as a point of persuasion, and I never really worried about, "Will this replicate or will this not?"' -- read by observers as very close to an admission of p-hacking. T8: the irony worth keeping: a paper about the impossible did more to reform a science than any paper about the possible, and historians of psychology date the replication crisis from it.
source: Wikipedia 'Daryl Bem' -- JPSP vol 100 no 3 (March 2011), nine experiments, erotic-image precognition and retroactive practice, the peer-review debate, the Ritchie/French/Wiseman replication rejected by JPSP, Science Brevia and Psychological Science 'on the grounds that it was a replication', the British Journal of Psychology referee episode, Wagenmakers' one-sided/two-sided p-value critique, Francis (2012) and Schimmack (2012) on the nine-of-ten rate, and Bem's 2017 Slate quotation with Vyse's assessment; Grokipedia 'Replication crisis' for the surrounding chronology.
framing_note: The catalyst ladder -- short, sharp, and the natural prerequisite for the p-hacking and file-drawer ladders. VOICE: this is a REVERSAL story told at the level of method rather than nature: the consensus overturned was psychology's confidence in its own toolkit. Present Bem without mockery -- he was doing what the field taught, and he said so. ACCURACY RAIL: Bem's paper has never been shown to be fraudulent and must not be called fraud; what failed is replication, and the rungs must say 'nobody has reproduced it' rather than 'he faked it'. The Slate quotation is documented -- reproduce it exactly as printed or paraphrase clearly; never invent a quote. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF: T4/T5 -- three journals refusing the replication because it was a replication, and then Bem refereeing it. That is the whole crisis in one anecdote. DISTRACTOR MINE: real adjacent parapsychology and its real critics (J.B. Rhine's Duke card experiments, the Ganzfeld debates, James Randi's prize) plus real methodological critics by name (Wagenmakers, Simonsohn, Schimmack, Francis) and real journals -- all live, none jokes. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: describe the SCENE (a flagship journal, nine experiments, a curtain on a screen) and let the reasoning move -- 'the method, not the finding, is what got tested' -- be the recalled answer; never state the reductio in the stem and ask what it was.
history_overlap: PHILOSOPHY bank owns reductio ad absurdum as an abstract reasoning move -- this ladder keys the actual 2011 episode and the three named rejections; leave the logical form to philosophy. No sister-bank fact duplicated.

name: P-hacking and the garden of forking paths
scope: How flexibility manufactures significance -- with no fraud required. T1: in 2011 three psychologists (Joseph Simmons, Leif Nelson and Uri Simonsohn) published a real experiment 'showing' that listening to the Beatles' 'When I'm Sixty-Four' made listeners about a year and a half YOUNGER -- not feel younger; younger by date of birth (the hook is the impossible result). T2: they got it without faking a single number, using only choices every researcher makes -- which covariate to include, when to stop collecting, which comparison song to use, which measure to report -- and they named the resource: 'researcher degrees of freedom'. T3: their simulations showed that combining four ordinary flexibilities pushes the chance of a false positive from the advertised 5% to roughly 61%. The 5% was never real in practice. T4 (teach the term before testing it): a p-value is the chance of seeing data at least this extreme if nothing were going on -- it is NOT the chance the finding is true, and it says nothing about how big an effect is. p-hacking is pushing on the analysis until that number drops under 0.05. T5: the subtler and far more common version -- Andrew Gelman and Eric Loken's 'garden of forking paths' (American Scientist, 2014): the researcher runs only ONE analysis and sincerely believes it was the right one, but WHICH analysis looked right was decided after seeing the data. No cheating occurred, and the p-value is still meaningless. T6 (the demonstration): Silberzahn and colleagues handed 29 independent teams the same football dataset and one question -- do referees show more red cards to dark-skinned players? Twenty of the 29 teams found a significant effect and nine did not, with odds ratios spread from 0.89 to 2.93. Same data, opposite headlines, everyone competent. T7: HARKing -- Hypothesizing After the Results are Known: writing the prediction after seeing the answer and presenting it as a prediction. A test you design after seeing the result is not a test. T8: optional stopping -- if you check the p-value after every new subject and stop the moment it dips under 0.05, you can reach 'significance' on pure noise given enough patience. T9 (the self-inflicted exposure): in November 2016 Cornell food researcher Brian Wansink published a blog post praising a graduate student who 'never said no', describing how he had sent her back into a failed pizza-buffet dataset until five papers came out of it. Outside statisticians read the post as a confession and went looking. T10: what they found -- Tim van der Zee, Jordan Anaya and Nick Brown identified roughly 150 impossible or inconsistent numbers in the pizza papers; Cornell found academic misconduct on 20 September 2018; more than twenty of Wansink's papers were retracted or corrected and he resigned in 2019 -- having previously run the USDA office that produced the 2010 Dietary Guidelines. T11: the survey nobody wants to read -- in an anonymous 2012 survey of more than 2,000 psychologists, 63% admitted failing to report all of a study's measures and about half admitted reporting only the analyses that 'worked'. These were not rare crimes; they were normal practice. T12: the one-sentence cure -- the only way anyone can tell whether an analysis was a prediction or a story is if it was written down BEFORE the data existed.
source: Grokipedia 'Replication crisis' -- researcher flexibility raising false positives to ~60%+, HARKing and optional stopping defined, John et al. 2012 survey figures (63% failing to report all dependent measures, ~50-56% selective reporting, 94% admitting at least one QRP), Brodeur et al. p-value bunching in economics; Wikipedia 'Data dredging' -- optional stopping, multiple testing, researcher degrees of freedom, remedies; Wikipedia 'Brian Wansink' -- the bottomless-bowl study, the blog post about the student who 'never said no', van der Zee/Anaya/Brown and the ~150 questionable numbers, Cornell's 20 September 2018 misconduct finding, 20+ retractions/corrections, 2019 resignation, USDA CNPP 2007-2009; Gelman & Loken, 'The garden of forking paths' (Columbia working paper / American Scientist 2014) -- the 'only ONE analysis' formulation and the ovulation-and-voting, ovulation-and-clothing-colour, arm-circumference-and-politics, beauty-and-sex-of-children examples; primary to verify: Simmons, Nelson & Simonsohn, Psychological Science 22(11):1359-1366 (2011); Silberzahn et al., Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science 1(3) (2018).
framing_note: The analytic backbone of the sub-strand -- theme ladder with a native T4/T5 ceiling. VOICE: the recognition skill is that this needs NO villain; T5 (forking paths) is the rung that makes the whole ladder honest, because it shows a sincere researcher producing a false positive. VERIFY AT BUILD (two figures I could not open the primary for): the '1.5 years younger' result and the 61% false-positive simulation in Simmons et al. 2011, and the 29 teams / 20-of-29 / OR 0.89-2.93 spread in Silberzahn et al. 2018. Do not seed a rung on either number until the primary paper is checked. ACCURACY RAILS: (1) Simmons et al. ran their Beatles study as a deliberate DEMONSTRATION and disclosed it as such in the same paper -- never present it as an accidental discovery or as fraud. (2) Wansink was found by Cornell to have committed academic misconduct; he was not criminally charged, and the finding concerns METHOD -- no rung may extend it into claims about what people should eat. (3) Teach 'p-value' at T4 before any rung tests reasoning about it. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF: T1 (music that changes your birth date) and T9 (the boss who publicly praised the student who never said no). DISTRACTOR MINE: the other real QRPs, each true and adjacent -- HARKing, optional stopping, outlier exclusion, subgroup slicing, dropping a condition, covariate shopping -- plus real statistical remedies a player might mis-pick (Bonferroni correction, funnel plot, p-curve, trim-and-fill, cross-validation) and real named statisticians (Fisher, Neyman, Rosenthal, Gelman, Simonsohn). LANE BORDER: the COOKING bank owns food knowledge and eating behaviour -- the Wansink rungs key the method collapse only.
history_overlap: COOKING bank owns food-and-eating knowledge -- the Wansink rungs (T9, T10) must key the METHOD collapse (the blog post, the 150 impossible numbers, the misconduct finding), never the diet advice or the bottomless-bowl result as nutrition. MATH bank owns probability drills -- keep T4's p-value teaching anchored to the named studies rather than becoming a statistics lesson.

name: The file drawer
scope: Why the literature is a highlight reel. T1: in 1979 Harvard psychologist Robert Rosenthal gave the thing that eats the evidence its name -- the 'file drawer problem': the studies that found nothing, were never written up, and sit in a drawer forever. T2: the consequence is structural, not moral -- a journal shelf is not a record of what was TESTED, only of what WORKED, and no reader can see the difference. T3 (the payoff measurement): Erick Turner and colleagues, writing in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2008, went to the FDA's registry of 74 antidepressant trials covering 12,564 patients -- registered before anyone saw the results, so nothing could hide. The FDA judged 51% of those trials positive. The published literature showed 94% positive. T4: how the gap was manufactured -- all 37 FDA-positive trials were published; of the 36 the FDA judged negative or questionable, 22 were never published at all, and 11 more WERE published, written up as though they had come out positive. T5: the size of the distortion -- the drugs' apparent effect was inflated by 32% overall, and by as much as 69% for individual drugs. T6: the honest consequence -- the doctor writing the prescription read the shelf, not the registry. This is how an entire profession can be sincerely misled without one fabricated number. T7 (the geography test, a superb single fact): a 1998 review found that no trial published in China, or in Russia and the USSR, had ever reported a tested treatment to be ineffective. A 100% success rate is not a scientific finding; it is a publishing policy. T8: who actually fills the drawer -- when researchers tracked a set of funded studies from grant to fate, most null results were never even written up. The censorship is largely self-administered by authors who correctly expect rejection. T9: the pharmaceutical version at scale -- governments stockpiled billions of dollars of the flu drug oseltamivir (Tamiflu); Cochrane reviewers spent years demanding the unpublished trial reports from the manufacturer, and when the full data finally arrived the claimed benefit shrank to roughly a day less of symptoms. T10: the repair that works -- prospective trial registration: from September 2004 the major medical journals announced they would not publish a trial unless it had been registered publicly BEFORE enrolling patients. You cannot quietly bin a study you were required to announce. T11: the recognition skill -- when someone says 'study after study shows', the question is not how many studies SHOW it, but how many were RUN.
source: PubMed abstract of Turner, Matthews, Linardatos, Tell & Rosenthal, NEJM 358:252-260 (2008) -- 74 FDA-registered trials, 12,564 patients, 12 agents, 51% positive by FDA vs 94% positive in print, 37 of 37 positive trials published, 22 negative never published and 11 published as positive, effect-size inflation 11-69% by drug and 32% overall; Wikipedia 'Publication bias' -- Rosenthal 1979 coining the 'file drawer problem', the September 2004 ICMJE registration requirement, the ~3x publication advantage for significant results, and the 1998 acupuncture-trial finding that no trial published in China or Russia/USSR found a treatment ineffective; Grokipedia 'Replication crisis' -- publication bias as a driver, funnel plots and Egger's test, trim-and-fill; verify at build: Franco/Malhotra/Simonovits (Science, 2014) TESS figures and the Cochrane/Roche oseltamivir review figures.
framing_note: VISION-MANDATED: this is the bank's 'the literature is a filtered product' ladder, and the lean is institutional honesty -- selective publication is documented, measured, and it distorted real prescribing. Steel-man the other side: the journals were not conspiring, they were preferring novelty, and the authors themselves binned most of the nulls. PRESENT the record; do not preach. ACCURACY RAIL (the important one): Turner's finding is about the PUBLISHED RECORD, not about whether antidepressants help anyone -- no rung may slide from '94% looked positive' to 'the drugs do not work'. Say the numbers exactly (74 / 51% / 94% / 32%). VERIFY AT BUILD before seeding T8 and T9: the Franco et al. 2014 percentages and the Cochrane oseltamivir outcome -- both are real and well documented, but I could not open the primaries, so check before writing a rung on either. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF: T3 (51% in the registry, 94% on the shelf) and T7 (a country whose trials never fail). DISTRACTOR MINE: real adjacent mechanisms that are NOT the file drawer -- funnel-plot asymmetry, Egger's test, trim-and-fill, the winner's curse, HARKing, industry sponsorship, small-study effects -- and real named reformers (Rosenthal, Iain Chalmers, Ben Goldacre and AllTrials, Tom Jefferson). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: describe the SCENE (a government registry that recorded every trial before it ran, set beside a library shelf) and let the 51/94 split be the recalled answer.
history_overlap: SCIENCE-INTERNAL: the vaccines sub-strand and the institutional-capture sub-strand own FDA/CDC/NIH capture, the revolving door, VAERS and the NCVIA -- this ladder keys SELECTIVE PUBLICATION only and must not re-tell those. Wakefield belongs to the vaccines sub-strand and must not appear here. The peer-review ladder in this same sub-strand owns Surgisphere -- do not duplicate it.

name: Peer review is a smell test, not a truth-detector
scope: What the gatekeeper has actually caught, and what it has missed. T1: in December 1912 Charles Dawson and the British Museum's Arthur Smith Woodward presented a skull to the Geological Society of London -- Eoanthropus dawsoni, 'Piltdown Man', the missing link, and conveniently the first Englishman. It stayed in the textbooks for forty-one years. T2: why the experts wanted it -- it fitted the reigning expectation that the human BRAIN enlarged first and the jaw modernized later, and it handed Britain a fossil to set beside France's and Germany's. T3 (the exposure, and a beautiful piece of chemistry): in 1953 Kenneth Oakley's fluorine-absorption test showed the skull and the jaw had lain in the ground for wildly different lengths of time; Joseph Weiner and Wilfrid Le Gros Clark then found FILE MARKS on the teeth and artificial staining. It was an orangutan's jaw joined to a human skull. T4: the modern coda -- a 2016 re-examination using CT scanning and DNA showed the teeth planted at both Piltdown sites came from the SAME orangutan: one forger, and the evidence points at Dawson. T5 (the correction most people need): peer review as we know it is YOUNG. Henry Oldenburg's Philosophical Transactions (1665) used trusted friends informally; external refereeing spread only after the Second World War, and Nature did not require external peer review until 1973. Newton, Darwin and Einstein published without it. T6: Einstein, 1936 -- he sent a paper to Physical Review, editor John Tate did the then-unusual thing of sending it to an anonymous referee, and Einstein wrote back that he had not authorized his manuscript to be shown 'to specialists before it is printed', withdrew it and published elsewhere. The sting in the tail: the referee had caught a genuine error, and Einstein quietly fixed the paper later. T7: what controlled tests show reviewers actually catch -- when researchers deliberately plant errors in a manuscript and send it out for review, reviewers find only about 20-33% of them. T8 (the sting): in 2013 John Bohannon, writing in Science, sent a fabricated paper about an anticancer molecule from a lichen -- with flaws bad enough that any competent reviewer should have stopped it -- to 304 open-access journals. 157 of them accepted it, including journals published by Elsevier and Sage. T9: the fraud review did not catch, part one -- Bell Labs physicist Jan Hendrik Schon was averaging a published paper every eight days in 2001. It was other scientists, reading closely -- Julia Hsu and Lynn Loo, then Lydia Sohn -- who noticed the SAME noise curve appearing in experiments supposedly run at different temperatures. The Beasley committee reported on 25 September 2002; about 25 papers were withdrawn, including seven from Nature and eight from Science. T10: part two -- Tilburg social psychologist Diederik Stapel simply invented his data for years, including a 2011 Science paper on messy environments and discrimination. He was caught by three junior researchers in his own department, one of whom said the numbers looked as if he had made them up himself; 58 papers were retracted. Review had stopped none of them. T11: part three, at speed -- in May 2020 The Lancet published a study reporting on 96,032 COVID patients from 671 hospitals, supplied by a company called Surgisphere, and the WHO paused a hydroxychloroquine trial arm on the strength of it. Outside readers noticed the Australian figures were impossible; the company turned out to have about eleven employees. The paper was retracted on 4 June 2020. T12: the pattern in one line -- in every one of these cases the catch came from OUTSIDE the review process: a reader with a ruler, a chemist with a spreadsheet, a graduate student who would not let it go. T13 (said fairly, and mandatory): what peer review IS good for -- controlled studies show reviewers reliably improve how a paper is written and how its methods are reported, and they do catch obvious blunders. It is a smell test performed by two or three busy strangers who never see your raw data. Useful. Not the same thing as true.
source: Grokipedia 'Peer review' -- Oldenburg's Philosophical Transactions 1665 and the post-WWII formalization, deliberate-error insertion studies with 20-33% detection rates, the Bohannon 2013 Science sting (304 open-access journals, 157 acceptances, Elsevier and Sage among them), the Surgisphere/Lancet paper (96,032 patients, 671 hospitals, retracted 4 June 2020, WHO trial pause), Wakefield's 12-child paper cited 1,000+ times after retraction, and the finding that review improves reporting quality; Wikipedia 'Scholarly peer review' -- Nature instituting formal peer review in 1967 and requiring external review in 1973, and Einstein's 1936 letter to John Torrence Tate Sr. quoted; Wikipedia 'Piltdown Man' -- Dawson and Woodward 1912, Eoanthropus dawsoni, the brain-first expectation and the 'first Briton' motive, Weidenreich's 1923 verdict, the 1953 Oakley/Weiner/Le Gros Clark fluorine exposure with file marks and staining, and the 2016 De Groote conclusion of a single forger; Wikipedia 'Jan Hendrik Schon' -- one paper per eight days in 2001, Hsu/Loo/Sohn spotting duplicated noise, Beasley report 25 September 2002 (misconduct in 16 of 24 allegations), ~25 retractions including 7 Nature and 8 Science, doctorate revoked 2004; Wikipedia 'Diederik Stapel' -- Tilburg, the 2011 Science paper, three junior whistleblowers, Levelt Committee, 58 retractions, PhD surrendered November 2011; Wikipedia 'Surgisphere'.
framing_note: VISION-MANDATED: this is the bank's 'peer review is not a truth-detector' ladder and it must land the point without becoming a sneer. T13 is MANDATORY and must be written as generously as the evidence allows -- reviewers demonstrably improve reporting, and a bank that says 'peer review is worthless' has taught the wrong lesson and armed the kid to dismiss anything he dislikes. The skill is calibration: know what the gate is FOR. ACCURACY RAILS (three): (1) Einstein's referee -- later identified as Howard Percy Robertson -- was RIGHT; Einstein's paper claimed gravitational waves do not exist and he corrected it afterwards. The anecdote is about NORMS being new, not about review being wrong; get this backwards and the rung teaches the opposite of the truth. Quote the 'to specialists before it is printed' phrase exactly as published in the Tate correspondence. (2) Piltdown: on the 2016 evidence Dawson is the leading suspect -- write 'the evidence points to Dawson', not 'Dawson was convicted'. (3) Bohannon's sting had no subscription-journal control group and was criticised for it -- if a rung uses it, it must key LAX REVIEW, not 'open access is worse'. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF: T3 (file marks on the teeth of the missing link) and T8 (157 of 304 journals said yes). DISTRACTOR MINE: real adjacent frauds and hoaxes -- Andrew Wakefield, Hwang Woo-suk's stem cells, Cyril Burt's twins, the Sokal hoax, the 1989 cold-fusion announcement -- and real detection tools that were NOT the one used (fluorine dating, image forensics and Elisabeth Bik, PubPeer, the GRIM test, carbon dating). Every option a real thing.
history_overlap: SCIENCE-INTERNAL: the COVID sub-strand owns Surgisphere as a POLICY story (the WHO Solidarity pause, hydroxychloroquine politics, the Proximal Origin duplicity) -- T11 here keys it strictly as a REVIEW failure (eleven employees, the impossible Australian numbers, thirteen days to retraction). The vaccines sub-strand owns Andrew Wakefield entirely with its two-direction context -- he may appear here only as a distractor option, never as a rung, and this ladder must not touch autism. HISTORY bank may own Piltdown as an Edwardian English episode -- this ladder keys the FLUORINE TEST, the file marks, and the forty-one-year miss, not the social history.

name: The law of small numbers
scope: Why a twenty-person study is usually noise -- and how to feel it in your own hands. T1 (kid-replicable hook): flip a coin ten times and you will fairly often get eight heads; flip it a thousand times and you will essentially never get eight hundred. Small samples do not merely carry more error -- they manufacture EXTREMES, at both ends. T2: in 1971 Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman handed a questionnaire to professional psychologists at their own conference and found the experts trusting small samples the way a gambler trusts a streak. They put the diagnosis in the title: 'Belief in the Law of Small Numbers' (Psychological Bulletin). T3 (the puzzle to pose): a large hospital records about 45 births a day, a small one about 15. Across a year, which records MORE days on which over 60% of the babies were boys? 56% of respondents answered 'about the same'; the correct answer is the small hospital, and it is not close. T4 (the sting in the real world): Wainer and Zwerling mapped kidney-cancer rates across US counties. The counties with the LOWEST rates are rural and thinly populated. So are the counties with the HIGHEST. Nothing about country living causes or prevents kidney cancer -- small counties simply swing further. T5: the same artifact convinced a generation of school reformers that SMALL schools produced the best results, because small schools topped the rankings -- as they also bottomed them -- and enormous sums went into breaking up large schools on the strength of a statistical mirage. T6: why this is the engine under the whole replication crisis -- a twenty-person study is a ten-coin-flip study. Jacob Cohen measured psychology's average statistical power in 1962 at about 0.46 for a medium effect; Sedlmeier and Gigerenzer measured it again across 1960-1987 and got 0.37. Two thirds of real effects were being missed. T7 (the mechanism, and the counter-intuitive part): the 'winner's curse' -- in an underpowered field the ONLY results that clear the significance bar are the ones chance pushed too far, so every published effect is systematically bigger than the real one. Median statistical power in neuroscience has been measured around 0.21, with published effects inflated up to threefold. T8 (the test-it-yourself close): before believing any headline effect, ask the number headlines never print -- how many people were in it? Then flip ten coins and remind yourself what noise looks like.
source: Wikipedia 'Insensitivity to sample size' -- Tversky & Kahneman, 'Belief in the law of small numbers', Psychological Bulletin 76(2):105-110 (1971); the hospital problem with the 45/15 births framing and the 56%/22%/22% response split; and Wainer & Zwerling on US counties showing both the lowest and the highest kidney-cancer rates as a sample-size artifact; Grokipedia 'Replication crisis' -- Cohen's 1962 power estimate of ~0.46, Sedlmeier & Gigerenzer's 1989 figure of 0.37 across 1960-1987, typical social-science power of 0.3-0.5, median neuroscience power of 0.21 and effect-size overestimation up to threefold, and the winner's-curse mechanism.
framing_note: The TEST-IT-YOURSELF ladder of the sub-strand: the coin-flip rung is the invitation, and it should be framed as an instruction, not an illustration -- go and do it tonight. VOICE: MECHANISM mode; the wonder is that a purely mathematical fact quietly wrecked a hospital study, a cancer map and a school-reform programme. ACCURACY RAIL: the hospital problem's answer is the SMALL hospital -- state the question exactly as Tversky and Kahneman posed it (over 60% boys, on how many days in a year) or the rung becomes unanswerable; and the kidney-cancer point is that small counties occupy BOTH extremes, so a rung that mentions only the low-rate half teaches the opposite lesson. VERIFY AT BUILD before seeding T5: the small-schools programme and its funder are real and well documented, but check the figures and the funder's name against a primary source before naming a dollar amount -- if it cannot be pinned down, write the rung without the number. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF: T4, the county map that says opposite things in the same colour. DISTRACTOR MINE: real adjacent statistical ideas that are NOT the answer -- regression to the mean, the gambler's fallacy, Simpson's paradox, selection bias, the central limit theorem, base-rate neglect -- each a genuine concept, several of them very nearly right, which is what makes the rung hard. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let a stem say 'small samples vary more' before asking about the counties -- describe the MAP (the healthiest counties and the sickest counties look the same) and let the cause be recalled.
history_overlap: MATH bank owns arithmetic and probability drills -- this is a wonder ladder anchored to named studies (the 1971 questionnaire, the hospital problem, the county cancer map, measured statistical power), never a statistics exercise. PHILOSOPHY bank may own base-rate neglect and the gambler's fallacy as reasoning moves -- keep those out of the stems here and use them only as distractors.

name: The repairs that actually work
scope: Science fixing its own method in public -- the anti-nihilism ladder. T1: the most powerful reform in modern method is a piece of paper. Write down your hypothesis, your sample size and your exact analysis BEFORE you collect a single data point, publish that document with a timestamp, and you have preregistered; the Open Science Framework has hosted these since 2013. T2: why so simple a thing works -- it makes the difference between a prediction and a story visible to a stranger. You may still explore the data afterwards; you must merely say which part was which. T3: the stronger version, invented by Chris Chambers at the journal Cortex in 2013 -- the Registered Report. The journal peer-reviews your QUESTION and your METHOD before you run the study and accepts it in principle, so the paper appears whether the answer comes out yes or no. T4 (the payoff number): about 96% of ordinary psychology papers report a positive result. Among Registered Reports -- where the journal committed before anyone knew the answer -- only about 44% do (Scheel, Schijen and Lakens, 2021). T5: what that gap MEANS: more than half of the 'findings' in the ordinary literature were never findings at all; they were the survivors of a selection process nobody could see. T6: multi-lab replication as standard equipment -- Many Labs 2 (2018) ran 28 classic effects across 28 laboratories on more than fifteen thousand people, and produced something more useful than a pass rate: effects that replicated replicated nearly everywhere, and effects that failed failed nearly everywhere. T7: adversarial collaboration -- Daniel Kahneman's method for a fight worth having: the two researchers who disagree design ONE experiment together, write down in advance what each possible result would mean, and run it, sometimes with a neutral arbiter. Nobody gets to explain the outcome away afterwards, because both sides signed for it first; Philip Tetlock and Cory Clark have institutionalized it in Penn's Adversarial Collaboration Project. T8: the fight over the threshold itself -- the American Statistical Association issued a formal statement in 2016 saying a p-value measures neither the size of an effect nor the probability that a hypothesis is true; in 2017 a group of 72 researchers proposed dropping the bar for claiming a new discovery from 0.05 to 0.005. T9: the plumbing that makes checking possible -- the Transparency and Openness Promotion guidelines (2015) let a journal state exactly what it demands (data, code, materials, preregistration), and the Retraction Watch database (2010) makes withdrawn papers findable instead of quietly vanishing. T10: who paid, and why that matters -- the Center for Open Science was founded in 2013 by Brian Nosek, and much of the money for replication came from private philanthropy, because the ordinary grant system rewards new findings and not checked ones. Fixing the incentive turned out to be harder than fixing the statistics. T11: the evidence the repair is working -- psychology studies published since 2015 run larger samples and report more modest effects. The literature got less exciting and more true, and that is the answer to the crisis: not less science, more checking, done in the open. T12 (the transferable habit): before running your own test, write down what result would prove you WRONG. If no result could, you do not have a test.
source: Grokipedia 'Replication crisis' (Remedies section) -- OSF preregistration from 2013, result-blind review proposed 2013 and Registered Replication Reports at Psychological Science from 2013, Registered Reports adopted at 200+ journals by the 2020s, the 2017 proposal by 72 researchers to move the threshold from 0.05 to 0.005, the ASA's 2016 statement on p-values, the TOP Guidelines (2015, updated 2024), the Retraction Watch Database (2010), Many Labs 2 (28 laboratories, 28 effects, ~50%), Templeton and NSF funding of replication work, and the 2025 meta-analyses showing larger samples and fewer questionable p-values; Wikipedia 'Registered report' -- Chris Chambers at Cortex in 2013, the two-stage review, Nature adopting the format in 2023, and Scheel/Schijen/Lakens 2021 giving ~96% positive results in standard psychology articles against ~44% of hypotheses in Registered Reports; Wikipedia 'Adversarial collaboration' -- Kahneman coining the term in the late 1990s, the 1988 Erez-Latham-Locke precedent, and the Adversarial Collaboration Project at Penn under Philip Tetlock and Cory Clark.
framing_note: VISION-MANDATED and structurally essential: this ladder is the guard rail that stops the whole sub-strand from teaching cynicism. The lean the bank owns here is that the Western scientific tradition is SELF-CORRECTING in public, and that the answer to bad science is more and better science -- named people, named journals, named documents. VOICE: DISCOVERY mode applied to method; the wonder is that so plain a device (write it down first) exposed so much. ACCURACY RAIL: the 96%-versus-44% comparison is a correlation between two different literatures, not a controlled experiment -- Scheel and colleagues say so themselves -- so no rung may claim preregistration CAUSED the drop; write it as 'when journals committed before knowing the answer, the positive-result rate fell to 44%'. Also do not imply preregistration is mandatory or universal; it is not. VERIFY AT BUILD: the exact ASA 2016 wording, the author count on the 2017 threshold proposal, and Many Labs 2's participant total. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF: T4 -- 96% against 44% -- and T12, which is the rung a father can hand a ten-year-old before a science-fair project. DISTRACTOR MINE: other real reforms a player could plausibly pick -- open data mandates, blinded analysis, p-curve, Bayes factors, post-publication review on PubPeer, multi-lab consortia, replication prediction markets -- and real named reformers (Nosek, Chambers, Simonsohn, Lakens, Kahneman, Tetlock, Ioannidis). LANE BORDER: philosophy owns Popper and Kuhn as epistemology -- this ladder keys WORKING PRACTICE, i.e. what a preregistration document literally contains and what a Stage 1 acceptance literally commits a journal to.
history_overlap: PHILOSOPHY bank owns Popper's falsification and Kuhn's paradigms as seminar epistemology -- T12's 'what would prove me wrong' rung must be framed as laboratory practice (a line written in a preregistration before data exist), not as the demarcation criterion. SCIENCE-INTERNAL: the biomedical-audit ladder in this sub-strand owns the NIH's 2015 rigour-and-authentication grant requirements -- do not duplicate them here.

name: Six out of fifty-three: when industry checked the biology
scope: The replication crisis where the money and the patients are. T1: around 2011-2012 two pharmaceutical companies quietly tried to build drug programmes on published academic biology and discovered they could not. Amgen's C. Glenn Begley and Lee Ellis reported in Nature that of 53 landmark preclinical cancer papers, only 6 could be confirmed -- 11%. T2: Bayer's team reported the same thing independently and earlier: only about a quarter of 67 projects in oncology, cardiovascular disease and women's health were fully consistent with the published data. T3 (why these audits are unusually credible): these were not hostile critics. The companies had every commercial reason to WANT the published findings to be true -- they were spending money to build medicines on them. T4 (the most damning single fact in the sub-strand): the public version, the Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology, set out in 2013 to repeat 193 experiments from 53 high-profile papers. Its worst result had nothing to do with the outcomes -- NOT ONE of the 193 experiments was described in enough detail to repeat from the published paper alone, and 70% of them required writing to the original authors for reagents. T5: of the experiments the team did manage to complete, the effects came out roughly 85% smaller on average than in the originals. T6: the price tag -- an analysis put the annual United States spend on irreproducible preclinical research at around $28 billion, roughly half of preclinical spending. T7: why this rung matters more than the psychology ones -- a false preclinical result does not sit harmlessly on a shelf; it sets the direction of drug programmes, and the overwhelming majority of compounds that enter human trials never reach approval. T8 (the honest reading, mandatory): this is an argument for better biology, not for distrusting medicine; and the repairs were named in the same breath -- reporting standards, authentication of cell lines and reagents, and from 2015 the NIH requiring grant applicants to address rigour, resource authentication and prior-evidence strength.
source: Grokipedia 'Replication crisis' -- Begley & Ellis 2012 (6 of 53, 11%), the 2011 Bayer analysis by Prinz, Schlange & Asadullah (about 25% of 67 projects validated), the Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology launched 2013 by the Center for Open Science with Science Exchange, the ~$28 billion annual figure for irreproducible US preclinical research, the 2024 survey finding 72% of biomedical researchers agreeing the field faces a reproducibility crisis, and the NIH's 2014-2015 reproducibility guidelines requiring applicants to address rigour and resource authentication; Wikipedia 'Reproducibility Project' -- 193 experiments from 53 papers published 2010-2012, only 50 experiments from 23 papers completed, effect sizes 85% smaller on average, none of the papers with fully described protocols, and 70% of experiments requiring key reagents from the original authors; primary: Begley & Ellis, Nature 483:531-533 (2012).
framing_note: VISION-MANDATED: this is where the sub-strand's stakes stop being academic. The bank's lean is institutional honesty about biomedical research quality WITHOUT sliding into medical nihilism -- T8 is mandatory and must be as forceful as T4. VOICE: MECHANISM and REVERSAL, told through numbers a reader can hold; the wonder is that a paper can be published in a top journal and still not contain enough information for anyone on earth to repeat it. ACCURACY RAIL: the 11% figure is Amgen's INTERNAL audit and the underlying 53 papers were never individually named -- say 'Amgen's team reported' and do not attribute the failure to any specific paper. Likewise state the RP:CB result precisely: of 193 planned experiments, 50 from 23 papers were completed, and the protocol finding applies to all 193. Do NOT let any rung generalize this into 'cancer research is fake' or 'medicines do not work'. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF: T4 -- not one of 193 experiments could be repeated from the paper alone. DISTRACTOR MINE: real adjacent causes that competent people proposed for these failures -- cell-line contamination and misidentification, batch effects in reagents, mouse-strain differences, selective reporting of the best of six runs, low statistical power, animal-model translation failure -- every one a genuine and documented problem, several of them partly true, which is what makes the rung hard. Also real named auditors (Begley, Ellis, Prinz, Nosek, Errington) and real journals. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: describe the SCENE (a drug company's scientists trying and failing to build on papers they had paid to believe) and let the number be recalled.
history_overlap: SCIENCE-INTERNAL: the institutional-capture sub-strand owns the FDA/CDC/NIH revolving door and industry funding of regulators -- this ladder keys the AUDIT NUMBERS only (Amgen 6 of 53, Bayer's quarter, RP:CB's 193 experiments, the $28 billion). The file-drawer ladder in this same sub-strand owns Turner's antidepressant trials -- do not restate selective publication here. ANIMAL bank owns creature biology; the mouse-model and cell-line rungs here are METHOD facts, not animal facts.
